lessons.unit: Unit 1: Decimals
lessons.title: Recurring decimals and fractions
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a decimal that never ends be an exact fraction?
objectives: To understand how to convert recurring decimals into fractions and why the method works
successCriteria: All: say whether a fraction gives a terminating or recurring decimal
Most: convert recurring decimals with one or two repeating digits to fractions
Some: prove a recurring decimal equals a given fraction when the repeat starts later
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: computers store some fractions only approximately, which causes rounding errors
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: infinitely repeating patterns can still be exact, prompting reflection on the infinite and the exact knowledge of Allah

keywords.def: a decimal with digits that repeat for ever
a decimal that ends
show something must be true using algebra
a factor that is a prime number

hook.text: 0.999... (nines for ever) and 1: are they the same number or not? How could you decide?
hook.a: They are equal. If x = 0.999..., then 10x = 9.999..., so 9x = 9 and x = 1. Today's method proves it.

starter.q: Write 0.45 as a fraction in its simplest form.
Write 72 as a product of prime factors.

teach.heading: Terminating or recurring?
bullets: In simplest form, look at the denominator's prime factors
teach.note: 7/40: 40 = 2³ × 5, so terminating (0.175). 5/12: 12 = 2² × 3, so recurring.

teach.heading: One digit or two repeating
bullets: Multiply by 10 for one repeating digit, 100 for two
teach.note: 4MA1 asks pupils to show the algebra, not just state the answer.

model.problem: Convert 0.454545... to a fraction.

teach.heading: Repeat starting later
bullets: Make two numbers with the same repeating tail
teach.note: Choose 10x and 100x so the tails match.

model.problem: Convert 0.2333... to a fraction.

teach.heading: Common error
teach.note: Write the tails under each other to check.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: Which fraction equals 0.181818...?
check.why: 18/99 = 2/11. 18/100 and 9/50 are 0.18, which terminates.

practice.q: Convert 0.777... to a fraction.
Convert 0.363636... to a fraction.
Convert 0.8333... to a fraction.
Is 7/40 terminating? Give its decimal.

independent.q: Core: Convert to fractions in their simplest form: (a) 0.555... (b) 0.090909... (c) 0.1222... (d) 0.123123...
Extend (exam style, 3 marks): Prove algebraically that 0.3181818... = 7/22.
Stretch: Prove that 0.999... = 1.

exit.q: Convert 0.636363... to a fraction.
Which of 3/8, 5/12 and 7/20 gives a recurring decimal?
exit.a: 5/12 (its denominator has a factor 3)

lessons.homework: Convert 0.4444..., 0.272727..., 0.1555... and 0.142857142857... to fractions, showing the algebra each time.
lessons.send: Support: x, 10x, 100x frame with tails lined up. EAL: 'recurring', 'terminating', 'prove'. Stretch: three-digit repeats starting after two decimal places.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Special numbers, powers and roots
lessons.title: Prime factors, HCF and LCM
lessons.bigQuestion: How do prime factors reveal what two numbers share?
objectives: To understand how prime factorisation finds the HCF and LCM
successCriteria: All: write a number as a product of prime factors in index form
Most: find the HCF and LCM of two numbers from their prime factors
Some: solve HCF and LCM problems and reason with index form
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: gear wheels and repeating cycles meet again at the LCM
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the primes, the building blocks of every whole number, show order in mathematics

keywords.def: a prime number that divides exactly
using powers, such as 2³ × 3²
highest common factor
lowest common multiple

hook.text: Two bells ring every 12 and every 18 minutes. They ring together at 9:00. When will they next ring together, and how could you be sure without listing every time?
hook.a: At 9:36: the LCM of 12 and 18 is 36. Prime factors find it quickly.

starter.q: Write the first five multiples of 15.

teach.heading: Prime factorisation
bullets: Divide by primes until you reach 1
teach.note: Use a factor tree or repeated division.

model.problem: Write 360 as a product of prime factors in index form.

teach.heading: HCF and LCM from prime factors
bullets: HCF: lowest power of each shared prime
LCM: highest power of every prime

teach.heading: Problems
bullets: Largest equal groups or tiles: HCF
teach.note: Bells: LCM(12, 18) = 36 minutes.

model.problem: Two bells ring every 45 s and 60 s. They ring together at 12:00:00. When do they next ring together?

teach.heading: Common error
teach.note: Ask: does 2² × 3 × 5 contain 120?

misconception.right: Use 2³ from 120: LCM = 2³ × 3 × 5 × 7 = 840

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: Find the HCF of 2³ × 3² × 5 and 2² × 3³ × 7.
check.why: Shared primes 2 and 3 at lowest powers: 2² × 3² = 36. The second option is the LCM.

practice.q: Write 252 as a product of prime factors.
Find the HCF of 48 and 180.
Find the LCM of 48 and 180.
Find the LCM of 15 and 20.

independent.q: Core: (a) Write 600 in index form. (b) Find the HCF and LCM of 72 and 84.
Extend (exam style, 3 marks): Tiles 84 cm by 120 cm are cut into identical squares as large as possible with no waste. Find the side of each square and how many there are.
Stretch: A = 2⁴ × 3 × 5² and B = 2² × 3³ × 5. Find the HCF and LCM in index form, and the smallest k such that Ak is a square number.

exit.q: Write 196 as a product of prime factors.
exit.a: 2² × 7²

exit.q: Find the HCF of 56 and 70.
Big question: what do the prime factors tell us about two numbers?
exit.a: Which building blocks they share (HCF) and the smallest number containing both (LCM).

lessons.homework: Find the HCF and LCM of 90 and 126, and of 2⁵ × 7 and 2³ × 3 × 7², showing prime factors.
lessons.send: Support: factor tree templates. EAL: 'factor', 'multiple', 'common'. Stretch: HCF and LCM of three numbers.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Special numbers, powers and roots
lessons.title: Negative and fractional indices
lessons.bigQuestion: What could a negative or a fractional power possibly mean?
objectives: To understand how negative and fractional indices follow from the index laws
successCriteria: All: evaluate negative indices as reciprocals
Most: evaluate fractional indices such as 27^(2/3)
Some: solve simple equations with indices by writing both sides with the same base
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: negative powers appear in units such as m s⁻¹ (metres per second)
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: following a pattern faithfully to discover new truths shows the reliability of reason

keywords.def: 1 divided by the number
a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ
a^(1/n) is the nth root of a
the number being raised to a power

hook.text: If 2³ = 8, 2² = 4, 2¹ = 2 and 2⁰ = 1, what should 2⁻¹ and 2^(1/2) be? How could the pattern decide?
hook.a: Each step down divides by 2, so 2⁻¹ = 1/2. And 2^(1/2) × 2^(1/2) = 2¹, so 2^(1/2) = √2.

teach.heading: The rules
teach.note: Each rule follows from the index laws. Evaluate the root first to keep numbers small.

teach.heading: Fractional indices
teach.note: Pupils then try 125^(2/3) (25).

model.problem: Evaluate 27^(2/3).

teach.heading: Negative fractional indices
teach.note: Flip fractions for a negative power.

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: A negative index does not make a negative number
teach.note: Ask: is 5⁻² bigger or smaller than 1?

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: Evaluate 64^(2/3).
check.why: ∛64 = 4 and 4² = 16. 42.67 is 64 × 2/3; 1/16 would need a negative index.

practice.q: Evaluate 3⁻².
Evaluate 49^(1/2).
Evaluate 125^(2/3).
Evaluate 81^(−1/4).

independent.q: Extend (exam style, 2 marks): Write √8 as a power of 2, and solve 4ˣ = 8.
Stretch: Solve 9^(x + 1) = 27ˣ.

exit.q: Evaluate 16^(3/4).
Evaluate 10⁻³.
Big question: what does a fractional index mean?
exit.a: A root: the denominator gives the root, the numerator the power.

lessons.homework: Evaluate 8^(−2/3), 0.25^(−1/2), (16/81)^(3/4) and 1^(−5); show the root step each time.
lessons.send: Support: rules card and roots table (squares and cubes). EAL: 'reciprocal', 'root', 'index'. Stretch: simplify algebraic expressions such as (8x⁶)^(2/3).

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Special numbers, powers and roots
lessons.title: Simplifying surds and rationalising the denominator
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do mathematicians prefer √2 to 1.41421...?
objectives: To understand how to simplify surds and rationalise denominators
successCriteria: All: simplify surds such as √72 = 6√2
Most: add, multiply and divide surds and rationalise a simple denominator
Some: rationalise a denominator of the form a ± √b
lessons.crossCurricular: Design: paper sizes A4 and A3 have sides in the ratio 1 : √2
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: exact answers such as √2 are perfect where decimals only approximate

keywords.def: a root that cannot be written exactly as a fraction, such as √2
take out square factors: √72 = 6√2
remove the surd from the denominator
not rounded

hook.text: A square has area 2 cm². How long is its side? Can you ever write the answer exactly as a decimal?
hook.a: √2 cm. Its decimal never ends or repeats, so √2 is the only exact way to write it.

starter.q: List the square numbers up to 100.

teach.heading: Simplifying surds
teach.note: Pupils then simplify √45 (3√5).

model.problem: Simplify √72.

misconception.right: √9 + √16 = 3 + 4 = 7: roots do not add like that

teach.heading: Rationalising
bullets: Multiply top and bottom by the surd
teach.note: Pupils then do 8/√2 (4√2).

model.problem: Rationalise 10/√5.

teach.heading: Denominators a ± √b
teach.note: The middle terms cancel, leaving a whole number.

model.problem: Rationalise 4/(3 − √5).

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: Simplify √48.
check.why: 48 = 16 × 3, so 4√3. 2√12 is not fully simplified (12 still has a square factor 4).

practice.q: Simplify √45.
Work out √12 × √3.
Simplify √75 − √27.
Rationalise 8/√2.

independent.q: Core: Simplify (a) √200 (b) √20 + √80 (c) 15/√5 (rationalise) (d) √6 × √15
Extend (exam style, 3 marks): A rectangle is √18 cm by √8 cm. Find its area and its perimeter in simplest form.
Stretch: Rationalise and simplify 6/(√3 + 1).

exit.q: Simplify √98.
Rationalise 12/√3.
Big question: why keep answers as surds?
exit.a: A surd is exact; its decimal never ends, so any decimal is rounded.

lessons.homework: Simplify √32, √108, √8 + √50 and 9/√3; check each with a calculator.
lessons.send: Support: list of square numbers to find square factors. EAL: 'surd', 'exact', 'rationalise'. Stretch: expand (2 + √3)² and (√5 − 1)(√5 + 3).

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Number: decimals, powers and roots
lessons.title: Expanding brackets with surds and rationalising
lessons.bigQuestion: Why would anyone want to remove a surd from the bottom of a fraction?
objectives: Expand brackets containing surds
Rationalise denominators of the form a/√b
Rationalise denominators of the form a/(b + √c)
successCriteria: Expand √2(3 + √2)
Rationalise 6/√3
Rationalise 4/(3 − √5) using the conjugate

lessons.smsc: Spiritual: perseverance with multi-step methods

keywords.def: remove the surd from the denominator
the same expression with the sign between terms changed, e.g. 3 + √5 → 3 − √5
not rounded
(a + b)(a − b) = a² − b²

teach.heading: Rationalising a/√b
teach.note: 6/√3 = 6√3/3 = 2√3. Answer the big question: exact values are easier to compare and add when the denominator is rational.

teach.heading: Using the conjugate
bullets: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate
The bottom becomes a difference of two squares
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Rationalise 4/(3 − √5)

teach.heading: Only multiplying the bottom
bullets: Top and bottom must be multiplied together
teach.note: Show how multiplying only the denominator changes the number.

teach.heading: Check: rationalise
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: Rationalise 10/√5
check.why: 10√5/5 = 2√5. A forgets the surd on top; C forgets to divide by 5.

practice: Expand √3(4 + √3)
Expand (1 + √2)²
Rationalise 8/√2
Rationalise 1/(2 + √3)

lessons.title: Expanding two and three binomials
lessons.bigQuestion: What shape does the expansion of three brackets describe?
objectives: Expand the product of two binomials
Expand the product of three binomials
Simplify the results
successCriteria: Expand (2x − 3)(x + 4)

an expression with highest power 3
multiply out brackets
terms with the same letters and powers

bullets: Multiply the result by the third
teach.note: Answer the big question: a cubic can describe a volume, e.g. a box with sides (x + 1), (x + 2), (x − 3).

model.problem: Expand (x + 1)(x + 2)(x − 3)

teach.note: Show me on 3.

lessons.unit: Unit 9: Algebraic manipulation
lessons.title: Expanding and factorising quadratics x² + bx + c
lessons.bigQuestion: How are expanding and factorising two sides of one idea?
objectives: To understand how to expand double brackets and factorise quadratic expressions
successCriteria: All: expand (x + a)(x + b)
Most: factorise x² + bx + c with positive and negative terms, and the difference of two squares
Some: factorise ax² + bx + c and use factorising to solve
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: projectile and area problems lead to quadratic expressions
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: al-Khwarizmi's work on squares and roots (الجبر) began the study of quadratics

keywords.def: an expression with x² as the highest power
multiply out brackets
write as a product of brackets
a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b)

hook.text: A rectangle has area x² + 7x + 12. What could its side lengths be? Is there more than one answer?
hook.a: (x + 3) and (x + 4), because they multiply to x² + 7x + 12. With whole-number terms this is the only pair.

starter.q: Find two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7.
Find two numbers that multiply to −15 and add to −2.

teach.heading: Expanding double brackets
bullets: Multiply every term by every term
teach.note: Grid for (x + 5)(x − 2): x², −2x, 5x, −10.

teach.heading: Factorising x² + bx + c
bullets: Find two numbers: product c, sum b
teach.note: Pupils then try x² + 9x + 20.

model.problem: Factorise x² − 2x − 15.

teach.heading: Difference of two squares
teach.note: The middle terms cancel when expanded.

model.problem: Factorise 2x² + 7x + 3.

bullets: Signs: product and sum both matter
teach.note: Check: −2 × 3 = −6, not +6.

teach.heading: Check

check.q: Factorise x² + x − 12.

Factorise x² + 2x − 24.
Factorise x² − 36.

islamicLink.text: Algebra takes its name from al-jabr (الجبر) in the book of Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, written in Baghdad in the 9th century. He described completing and balancing equations to solve problems of inheritance and trade, the same methods we use today.

Use the product rule to count combinations (Higher)
Decide when repeats are or are not allowed
successCriteria: All: list outcomes in a sensible order
Most: use the product rule for independent choices
Some: count arrangements where repeats are not allowed or there is a condition
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: passwords and combinations; Business: menu and product choices
lessons.smsc: Moral: order and care in work so that nothing is overlooked

keywords.def: one possible result
done in an organised order
multiply the number of choices at each stage
a selected set of choices

starter: How many outcomes when a coin is flipped once?

teach.heading: Systematic listing
bullets: Fix the first item, then vary the next
Check the total at the end
Foundation: list all three-digit numbers from the digits 1, 2, 3 without repeats
teach.note: List: 123, 132, 213, 231, 312, 321 = 6. Show that fixing the first digit gives 2 each time. Pupils compare unorganised lists to see how items are missed.

teach.heading: The product rule
bullets: Number of choices at each stage
It works when choices are independent
teach.note: Use an iftar box: 3 types of samosa, 4 drinks, 2 desserts. Ask why we do not add: every starter can be paired with every main.

model.problem: A code is 4 digits from 0–9. How many codes if digits can repeat, and if they cannot?

teach.heading: Adding instead of multiplying
bullets: Choices at different stages multiply, they do not add
teach.note: Ask pupils to list a small case (2 shirts, 3 scarves) to see 6 outfits, not 5.

misconception.right: 3 × 4 = 12 meals, one starter with one main each time

teach.heading: Conditions and constraints
bullets: Deal with the restricted place first
Even number: last digit must be even
Example: 3-digit even numbers from 1–5, no repeats
Last digit 2 or 4: 2 ways; first 4 ways; second 3 ways
teach.note: Answer: 2 × 4 × 3 = 24. Emphasise choosing the most restricted position first.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards. Pupils must show the multiplication.

check.q: How many four-digit numbers can be made from 1, 2, 3, 4 using each digit exactly once?
check.why: 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24. D allows repeats (4⁴); B is 4 × 4.

practice: List all the two-letter codes from A, B, C where repeats are allowed. How many?
A café has 5 sandwiches and 3 drinks. How many meal deals?
How many 3-digit numbers from 1–9 have no repeated digit?
independent: Core: (a) 6 trousers × 4 tops (b) list the outcomes when two coins are flipped
Extend: A plate has 2 letters then 3 digits. How many plates (letters A–Z, digits 0–9, repeats allowed)? How many with no repeats at all?
Stretch: How many 3-digit odd numbers use only digits 1–6 with no repeats? Show a structured method.
exit: How many outfits from 4 scarves and 3 coats?
List all arrangements of the letters X, Y, Z.
Return to the big question: 3 samosas, 4 drinks, 2 desserts.
lessons.homework: Six counting questions, two requiring systematic lists and four using the product rule, including a contextual question about a PIN.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: tree diagrams and highlighted fixed items; stretch: factorial notation n! and arrangements of letters with repeats.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: N1-N9 Number: structure and calculation
lessons.title: Powers, roots, estimating and the laws of indices
lessons.bigQuestion: How can you estimate a square root without a calculator?
objectives: Recall squares, cubes and their roots
Estimate roots and powers
Use the laws of indices with positive integers
successCriteria: All: recall squares to 15² and cubes
Most: estimate surds between two integers
Some: simplify expressions using index laws including brackets
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: area, volume and scale; Computing: powers of 2
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: patterns in numbers show order and design

keywords.def: how many times a number is multiplied by itself
the inverse of a power
rules for combining powers of the same base
find an approximate answer

starter: Between which two whole numbers does 40 lie, relative to square numbers?

teach.heading: Know your squares and cubes
bullets: Recall speeds up all index work
teach.note: Use a rapid-fire quiz. Ask: what is the difference between 2³ and 3²? (8 and 9).

teach.heading: Estimating roots
teach.note: Say why √50 is close to 7: 50 is close to 49. Then model on √72.

model.problem: Estimate √72 to one decimal place

teach.heading: Index laws (positive integers)
bullets: Apply to numbers and to letters
teach.note: Examples: (2³ × 2⁵)/2⁴ = 2⁴ = 16; (3²)³ = 3⁶ = 729; 3x²y × 4xy³ = 12x³y⁴. Separate the coefficient work from the letters.

teach.heading: Brackets and powers
teach.note: A very common error is to leave the coefficient uncubed.

misconception.right: (2a)³ = 2³ × a³ = 8a³

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: Which is closest to √72?
check.why: 8.5² = 72.25. D halves 72 rather than rooting; A and C are too far from 72 when squared (56.25 and 90.25).

practice: Simplify 5⁴ × 5² and 7⁸ ÷ 7⁵
Estimate √90 between two integers, then to 1 d.p.
Simplify (2x³)³ and 4a²b × 3ab⁴
Work out (2⁵ × 2³)/2⁶
independent: Core: (a) 9² (b) ∛125 (c) 2³ × 2⁴ (d) y⁵ ÷ y² (e) (x²)⁴
Extend: Between which consecutive integers is ∛100? Estimate it to 1 d.p. without a calculator.
Stretch: Solve 2ⁿ × 4³ = 2¹¹ and (3ⁿ)² ÷ 3⁴ = 27.
exit: Simplify a⁴ × a³
Simplify (3b²)²
Estimate √30 to 1 d.p.
lessons.homework: Ten index-law and estimating-root questions; include (2x²)³ and one problem on estimating a cube root.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: laws card with one numerical example each. Stretch: show a⁰ = 1 using the division law.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: N1-N9 Number: structure and calculation
lessons.title: Exact calculations with π
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do mathematicians often leave π in an answer rather than using 3.14?
objectives: Give answers in terms of π
Find exact areas, circumferences and volumes
Work backwards from an area or circumference in terms of π
successCriteria: All: calculate the area and circumference of a circle in terms of π
Most: calculate semicircles, compound shapes and cylinders exactly
Some: work backwards and use π in ratios
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: circular motion, astronomy and engineering design
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: awe at a number with no end that perfectly describes every circle

keywords.def: not rounded; kept in terms of π or a surd
the distance around a circle, C = πd = 2πr
A = πr²
distance from centre to the edge

starter: Bismillah. What is the diameter of a circle with radius 7?
Write the formula for the area of a circle.

teach.heading: Why leave π?
bullets: π is irrational: its decimals never end
Leave π in the answer for an exact value
Round only at the very end
teach.note: Show that 12π is exact but 37.7 is rounded. Mention that the exact value is better for further calculations.

teach.heading: Area and circumference
bullets: Do not multiply by π unless asked
teach.note: Hinge: radius 6, so r² = 36 gives 36π cm².

model.problem: Find the perimeter of a semicircle of radius 5 cm, exactly

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: Square r first, then multiply by π
teach.note: Compare doubling and squaring.

misconception.right: Area = π × 4² = 16π

teach.heading: Working backwards
teach.note: Pupils divide by π before solving. Extension: ratio of the areas of two circles with radius 3 and 6 is 1 : 4.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: A circle has circumference 16π. What is its radius?
check.why: 2πr = 16π gives r = 8. A halves the radius again; C is just the number 16 in 16π; D doubles it.

practice: Exact area and circumference of a circle of radius 9 cm
Exact area of a semicircle of diameter 10 cm
A cylinder has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. Find its volume in terms of π.
A circle has area 64π. Find its circumference in terms of π.
independent: Core: Exact area and perimeter of a circle of radius 12 and of diameter 7.

Extend: A square of side 10 cm contains a quarter circle of radius 10 cm. Find the shaded area outside the quarter circle in exact form. Find the exact volume of a sphere of radius 6 using V = 4/3 πr³.
Stretch: Two circles have areas in ratio 4 : 9. Find the ratio of their circumferences and explain.
exit: Exact area of a circle with diameter 12 cm
Perimeter of a semicircle with radius 4 cm, exact
A circle has circumference 18π. Find the area, exactly.
lessons.homework: Six exact-answer questions on circles and cylinders, plus one question where answers are given as a multiple of π and then rounded to 3 s.f.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: formula card with worked radius 6 example. Stretch: arcs and sectors in terms of π.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: N1-N9 Number: structure and calculation
lessons.title: Standard form: writing and converting
lessons.bigQuestion: How can scientists write the distance to the Sun without a page of zeros?
objectives: Write large and small numbers in standard form
Convert standard form to ordinary numbers
Order numbers in standard form
successCriteria: All: write numbers such as 450 000 in standard form
Most: write numbers such as 0.00032 and convert back
Some: identify and correct numbers wrongly written in standard form
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: astronomy, atomic sizes; Computing: data storage
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflection on the vast and the tiny scales of creation

keywords.def: a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10 and n an integer
the power n in 10ⁿ
the digits that carry value
a rough size, the power of 10

teach.heading: The form a × 10ⁿ
bullets: n is a whole number, positive for large numbers, negative for small
teach.note: Method: place the decimal point after the first non-zero digit, count the moves. Moves left give positive n, moves right negative n.

model.problem: Write 0.00072 in standard form
steps: Move the point 4 places right to get 7.2
Moving right means the index is negative

teach.heading: Standard or not?
bullets: Fix by adjusting a and n together
teach.note: Convert 52.4 × 10³ to 5.24 × 10⁴. Ask why one decimal place movement changes the index by one.

teach.heading: Converting back
teach.note: Use zeros as placeholders. Check by estimating: does the answer feel large or small?

teach.heading: A common error
bullets: A negative index does not make the number negative
teach.note: Contrast 10⁻³ with −1000.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards: show a letter.

check.q: Which number is written in standard form?
check.why: Only 4.8 × 10⁻³ has 1 ≤ a < 10. A has a below 1; B and D have a above 10.

practice: Write 4 500 000 and 0.0063 in standard form
Write 7.2 × 10⁴ and 3 × 10⁻⁵ as ordinary numbers
Write 52.4 × 10³ in standard form
Put in order, smallest first: 3.1 × 10⁻², 2.9 × 10⁻³, 4.5 × 10⁻²
independent: Core: Write in standard form: 90 000, 0.07, 1 200 000, 0.000045.
Extend: The speed of light is about 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Write this as an ordinary number. A virus has width 1.2 × 10⁻⁷ m. Write this in ordinary form.
Stretch: Which is bigger, 6.2 × 10⁻⁵ or 0.00007? By how many times is 8 × 10⁶ bigger than 4 × 10³?
exit: Write 0.000038 in standard form
Write 2.4 × 10⁵ as an ordinary number
Is 14 × 10⁻³ in standard form? Correct it if not.
lessons.homework: Ten conversion questions, including at least four with negative indices and three in a scientific context.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: place-value grid with decimal point arrows; word bank for 'standard form'. Stretch: ordering numbers across mixed indices.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: N1-N9 Number: structure and calculation
lessons.title: Calculating with standard form
lessons.bigQuestion: Can we multiply the Earth's mass by a million without writing all those zeros?
objectives: Multiply and divide numbers in standard form
Add and subtract numbers in standard form
Use a calculator and interpret standard form in context
successCriteria: All: multiply numbers in standard form
Most: divide, and add or subtract using ordinary numbers or common powers
Some: interpret answers in context and give them to suitable accuracy
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: astronomical distances and atomic scales
lessons.smsc: Social: honesty in reporting calculations to a sensible accuracy

keywords.def: a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10
the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 × 10¹² km
digits counted from the first non-zero digit

teach.heading: Multiply and divide
bullets: Multiply the numbers, add the indices
Divide the numbers, subtract the indices
Adjust the result so a is between 1 and 10
teach.note: Slow the model down: separate the number parts and the powers of ten.

model.problem: Work out (6 × 10⁵) × (5 × 10³), giving a standard form answer

teach.heading: Dividing and small numbers
teach.note: Negative indices: −3 − 5 = −8. Re-normalise 0.4 into 4 with one lower index.

teach.heading: Adding and subtracting
bullets: Make the powers of ten the same
teach.note: Alternative: convert to ordinary numbers: 340 000 + 52 000 = 392 000. Warn that you cannot just add the indices.

misconception.right: 3 × 10⁴ + 2 × 10⁴ = 5 × 10⁴; the power stays the same

teach.heading: In context
bullets: Star at 4.2 × 10¹³ km; light travels 9.5 × 10¹² km per year
teach.note: Give the answer to 2 or 3 significant figures. Use the calculator's EXP key and check by estimation.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: Work out (4 × 10³) × (5 × 10⁶) in standard form
check.why: 4 × 5 = 20, 10³ × 10⁶ = 10⁹ so 20 × 10⁹ = 2 × 10¹⁰. A is not standard form; D adds the numbers.

practice: Work out (9 × 10⁶) ÷ (3 × 10²)
Work out 6.1 × 10⁴ + 3.9 × 10³
independent: Extend: A virus has width 1.2 × 10⁻⁷ m. How many fit across 3 × 10⁻³ m? Give your answer in standard form.
Stretch: A star is 4.2 × 10¹³ km away. A probe travels at 2.8 × 10⁵ km/h. Find the journey time in years (1 year = 8.76 × 10³ hours) to 2 s.f.
exit: Work out (3 × 10⁷) × (4 × 10³)
Work out (6 × 10⁹) ÷ (3 × 10⁴)
Work out 5.5 × 10⁵ − 5 × 10⁴
lessons.homework: Eight standard form calculations, including addition and subtraction, and a worded problem with an answer to 3 s.f.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: two-column method card 'numbers / powers'; calculator EXP key demo. Stretch: surd and standard form mixed problems.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: N10-N12 Number: fractions, decimals and percentages
lessons.title: Terminating decimals and fractions
lessons.bigQuestion: How can you tell, before dividing, whether a fraction will have a decimal that ends?
objectives: Convert terminating decimals to fractions in simplest form
Convert fractions to terminating decimals
Decide whether a fraction gives a terminating decimal from its denominator
successCriteria: All: convert simple decimals and fractions
Most: convert decimals such as 0.375 to fractions and divide to find 7/16
Some: use prime factors of the denominator to predict termination
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: measurements and data; Finance: prices and discounts
lessons.smsc: Social: precision and honesty in reporting measurements

keywords.def: a decimal that ends after a finite number of digits
a decimal with a repeating pattern that never ends
a fraction with the same value
the numerator and denominator have no common factor

starter: Write 80 as a product of prime factors.

teach.heading: Decimal to fraction
bullets: Use the place value of the last digit
teach.note: Link to place value columns: tenths, hundredths, thousandths. 2.4 = 2 4/10 = 2 2/5 = 12/5.

model.problem: Write 0.375 as a fraction in its simplest form

teach.heading: Fraction to decimal
bullets: Divide the numerator by the denominator
teach.note: Show short division with bus stop for 7 ÷ 16. For 9/25 scale to hundredths by multiplying top and bottom by 4.

teach.heading: Common error
teach.note: Ask for 1/8 first: 0.125, so 3/8 is three of them, 0.375.

teach.heading: Will it terminate?
bullets: Write the fraction in simplest form
Prime factors of the denominator only 2s and 5s: terminates
teach.note: Why: a terminating decimal is a fraction over 10, 100, 1000 …, and these only have 2 and 5 as prime factors. Recurring-decimal conversion is covered in the school's Year 10 'Recurring decimals and fractions' lesson.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: Which fraction gives a terminating decimal?
check.why: 40 = 2³ × 5 so 9/40 terminates (0.225). 12, 15 and 18 each have a factor of 3 that is not cancelled.

practice: Write 0.45, 0.0125 and 3.6 as fractions in simplest form
Write 5/8, 7/20 and 11/16 as decimals
Without dividing, which of 3/7, 11/20, 7/30 terminate?
Show that 21/70 gives a terminating decimal.
independent: Core: Convert 0.8, 0.35, 0.125 to fractions and 1/5, 3/4, 5/8 to decimals.
Extend: Write 2.64 as an improper fraction and explain whether 17/48 terminates.
Stretch: Find three fractions between 1/3 and 1/2 that give terminating decimals.
exit: Write 0.56 as a simplest fraction
Write 7/16 as a decimal
Will 5/12 terminate? Explain.
lessons.homework: Eight conversions plus two 'terminate or not?' questions with explanations using prime factors.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: place-value chart and bus-stop division frame. Stretch: predict the length of decimal for 1/7.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: N10-N12 Number: fractions, decimals and percentages
lessons.title: Fractions within ratio problems
lessons.bigQuestion: If a group shares in the ratio 3 : 2, what fraction does each person get?
objectives: Link ratios and fractions
Solve ratio problems that use fractions
Combine fractions of fractions
successCriteria: All: convert a ratio to fractions of the whole
Most: compare quantities given as fractions of each other
Some: solve multi-stage ratio and fraction problems
lessons.crossCurricular: Business: sharing profits; Science: mixtures and concentrations
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness ('adl) when sharing between people

keywords.def: a comparison of quantities in order
divide in a given ratio
multiply by that fraction
write with the smallest whole numbers

teach.heading: Ratio to fraction
teach.note: Emphasise: the fraction uses the total number of parts, not the other part.

teach.heading: Ratio from fractions
bullets: Write both as equivalent fractions with the same denominator
teach.note: Alternative: multiply both by the LCM 12.

model.problem: Find A : B if 2/5 of A equals 1/3 of B

teach.heading: Fractions of fractions
bullets: 3/5 take bus or bike in the ratio 3 : 2
teach.note: Draw a bar model with 5 parts, shade 3, then split the shaded part into 5 again.

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: Add the parts to find the total number of parts
teach.note: 1 : 3 means 1/4 and 3/4 of the whole.

misconception.wrong: In the ratio 1 : 3 the first part is 1/3 of the total
misconception.right: In the ratio 1 : 3 the first part is 1/4 of the total (4 parts in all)

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: In a bag, 3/7 of counters are red. The rest are blue and green in the ratio 1 : 3. What fraction of the bag is green?
check.why: Blue and green make 4/7. Green is 3/4 of that: 3/4 × 4/7 = 3/7. B is the blue fraction; C ignores the 4/7.

practice: Write the fractions of the whole in the ratio 4 : 7
Find the ratio 3/5 : 1/2
A bag has red and blue counters in the ratio 3 : 4. What fraction is blue? 14 are red: how many counters in total?
Of a class, 2/5 walk. The rest bus or cycle in the ratio 3 : 1. What fraction cycle?
independent: Core: (a) 2/3 : 5/6 (b) the fraction of 3 : 7 for each part (c) share £90 in ratio 2 : 3
Extend: A is 3/4 of B and B is 2/3 of C. Find A : B : C.
Stretch: In a school 3/5 of pupils are girls. 1/4 of the girls and 1/3 of the boys walk. What fraction of the school walks?
exit: Write 2 : 3 as fractions of the total
Simplify 1/4 : 2/3
Return to the big question: 3 : 2 gives what fractions?
lessons.homework: Six problems that mix ratio and fraction, including one three-stage problem in context (a mixed bag, a class).
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: bar models and part-whole diagrams; vocabulary 'of the total'. Stretch: algebraic ratio with fractions.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: Unit 4: Percentages
lessons.title: Percentages as multipliers; one quantity as a percentage of another
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a single decimal do the work of a percentage?
objectives: To understand how percentages act as multipliers and how to write one quantity as a percentage of another
successCriteria: All: write one quantity as a percentage of another, with units matched
Most: use a decimal multiplier to find a percentage of an amount
Some: combine percentages of percentages
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: percentage composition and percentage yield
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest reporting of results as percentages, without misleading comparisons

keywords.def: a decimal equal to a percentage, such as 0.35 for 35%
a part out of 100 of an amount
part ÷ whole × 100
must be the same before comparing

hook.text: Yusuf scored 34 out of 40 in Arabic and 41 out of 50 in maths. In which did he do better? How could you be sure?
hook.a: 34/40 = 85% and 41/50 = 82%, so Arabic. Percentages put different totals on the same scale.

teach.heading: As a percentage of
teach.note: 45 minutes as a percentage of 2 hours: 45 ÷ 120 × 100.

model.problem: Write 45 minutes as a percentage of 2 hours.

teach.heading: Multipliers
teach.note: 4MA1 1.6D: percentages as operators.

teach.heading: Common error
teach.note: Ask: is 350 g out of 2 kg really 175%?

misconception.wrong: 350 g as a percentage of 2 kg = 350 ÷ 2 × 100 = 17 500%

teach.heading: Percentage of a percentage
teach.note: x is 20% of y and y is 40% of z: 0.2 × 0.4 = 0.08.

model.problem: x is 20% of y, and y is 40% of z. What percentage of z is x?

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: What is 18 as a percentage of 72?
check.why: 18 ÷ 72 = 0.25 = 25%. 400% divides the wrong way.

practice.q: Write 34 out of 40 as a percentage.
Write 45 minutes as a percentage of 2 hours.
Work out 0.65 × 340.
Write 7/8 as a percentage.

independent.q: Core: (a) Write 27 out of 60 as a percentage. (b) Write 350 g as a percentage of 2 kg. (c) Use a multiplier to find 64% of 425.
Extend (exam style, 2 marks): In a survey, 156 of 240 households recycle glass. What percentage do not?
Stretch: A shop's price is 125% of the cost. In a sale the price is 80% of the shop's price. What percentage of the cost is the sale price?
independent.a: 1.25 × 0.8 = 1, so 100%: the sale price equals the cost

exit.q: Write 9 out of 12 as a percentage.
Work out 0.07 × 600.
Big question: why must units match?
exit.a: A percentage compares like with like; mixed units give a meaningless answer.

lessons.homework: Write five of your recent test scores as percentages and order them; use a multiplier to check one.
lessons.send: Support: part ÷ whole × 100 frame with units box. EAL: 'as a percentage of', 'multiplier'. Stretch: percentage composition by mass of water (H₂O: 2 g hydrogen in 18 g).

lessons.unit: Unit 4: Percentages
lessons.title: Repeated percentage change, compound interest and depreciation
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does repeated percentage change grow or shrink so quickly?
objectives: To understand how repeated percentage change works, including compound interest and depreciation
successCriteria: All: use multiplierⁿ for repeated change
Most: solve compound interest and depreciation problems in exam style
Some: find the rate or the number of years from given values
lessons.crossCurricular: Biology: bacterial growth is modelled with repeated percentage increase
lessons.smsc: Moral: seeing how debt grows under interest helps us understand one wisdom behind the prohibition of riba

keywords.def: the same percentage change applied again and again
interest added to the amount so later interest is on a bigger amount
a fall in value over time
رِبَا: an increase charged on a loan, forbidden in Islam

hook.text: A town of 25,000 people grows by 3% a year. Someone says that in 4 years it grows by 12%. Is that right? Why or why not?
hook.a: No: 1.03⁴ = 1.1255, a 12.55% rise (to about 28,138), because each year's 3% is of a bigger population.

starter.q: Write the multiplier for a 12% decrease.
After a 20% rise a price is £66. Original?

teach.heading: Repeated change
teach.note: Town of 25,000 growing 3% a year.

teach.heading: Depreciation
teach.note: Pupils then do £12,000 at 15% for 2 years (£8,670).

model.problem: A car costs £18,500 and depreciates by 12% a year. Find its value after 3 years.

teach.heading: Islamic note: riba
bullets: Islamic finance uses partnership and cost-plus sale instead
teach.note: Islamic note: riba (رِبَا) is forbidden (Qur'an 2:275: Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba). Islamic finance uses partnership (mushārakah, مُشَارَكَة) and cost-plus sale (murābaḥah, مُرَابَحَة) instead. 4MA1 examines compound interest (1.6), so we learn it accurately as knowledge of the wider economy, never as something to take.

quote.text: Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba.

teach.heading: Compound interest (exam knowledge)
bullets: Same method: multiplier 1 + r/100 to the power n
teach.note: Exam questions may say 'compound interest'; the method is repeated percentage change.

model.problem: In the wider economy, £4,000 grows at 2.5% compound interest a year. Find the amount after 5 years.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: Which gives the value of £600 after 5 years of 4% depreciation?
check.why: Each year keeps 96%, five times. 600 × 0.8 is a simple 20% drop.

practice.q: Increase 800 by 5% each year for 3 years.
A value of 12,000 falls by 15% a year. Find it after 2 years.
Write the single multiplier for 6 years of 2% decrease (4 d.p.).
A 10% rise is followed by a 20% fall. Find the overall percentage change.

independent.q: Core: (a) A machine worth £24,000 depreciates by 15% a year. Find its value after 4 years. (b) In the wider economy, £3,500 grows at 4% compound interest. Find the amount after 3 years.
Extend (exam style, 3 marks): A colony of 2,400 bacteria increases by 15% each hour. How many bacteria are there after 6 hours? Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
Stretch: A house rises in value by r% each year. In 2 years it goes from £250,000 to £275,625. Find r.

exit.q: A value of £5,000 falls by 10% a year. Find it after 3 years.
Big question: why is 3% a year for 4 years not 12%?
exit.a: Each year's 3% is of a bigger amount: 1.03⁴ = 1.1255, a 12.55% rise.

lessons.homework: For a £20,000 car losing 15% a year, find the first year its value is below £10,000, and the value then; show the multiplier method.
lessons.send: Support: year-by-year table before using powers. EAL: 'compound', 'depreciation', 'repeated'. Stretch: trial and improvement to find the years to halve at 8% a year.

A used car with a price sign

islamicLink.text: Islamic note: riba (رِبَا) is forbidden (Qur'an 2:275: Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba). Islamic finance uses partnership (mushārakah, مُشَارَكَة) and cost-plus sale (murābaḥah, مُرَابَحَة) instead. We learn how interest works as knowledge of the wider economy, never as something to take.

lessons.unit: A1-A7 Algebra: notation, vocabulary and manipulation
lessons.title: Algebraic notation and vocabulary
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do mathematicians agree on one language for algebra?
objectives: Write algebra using correct notation
Use the words expression, equation, formula, identity and inequality
Simplify by collecting like terms
successCriteria: All: write and simplify simple expressions
Most: classify an item as an expression, equation, formula, identity or inequality
Some: form and simplify expressions from words and diagrams
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: variables and expressions in code
lessons.smsc: Social: shared conventions let people from many places understand the same mathematics

keywords.def: terms combined with no equals sign, such as 3x + 2
a statement that two expressions are equal for particular values
a rule linking quantities, such as A = πr²
true for every value of the variable, written ≡
compares using < > ≤ ≥
a part of an expression separated by + or −

starter: What is the next term in 3, 7, 11, 15?
Write 'three more than a number' as a calculation.

teach.heading: Notation rules
bullets: a × a is a², a × a × a is a³
teach.note: Stress that we omit × signs and put the number first. Ask: what is the difference between 3a and a³?

model.problem: Write as simply as possible: 5 × a × b × 2 + a × a × 3
steps: The terms are unlike so cannot combine

teach.heading: Words of algebra
teach.note: Use a sorting task with five cards. Inequality: x > 4. Point out that a formula is also an equation with several letters.

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: Unlike terms cannot be combined: a and a² are different
teach.note: Test with a = 5: a + a = 10 but a² = 25.

misconception.right: a + a = 2a, while a × a = a²

teach.heading: Forming expressions
bullets: Perimeter of a rectangle with sides 2a and b: 4a + 2b
teach.note: Ask pupils to say each expression in words before writing it.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards: show a letter.

check.q: Which of these is an identity?
check.why: 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 is true for every x. A is an equation true only for x = 3; C is an inequality; D is a formula.

practice: Simplify 4a + 3b − a + 5b
Simplify 3x × 4y and 2a × a × 5
Classify: (i) 5x − 1 (ii) 5x − 1 = 14 (iii) v = u + at (iv) y < 7
Write an expression for the cost of 4 notebooks at £n and 3 pens at £p.
independent: Core: Simplify (a) 7x + 2x (b) 3a + 4b − a (c) 5ab + 2ba
Extend: Write expressions for the area and the perimeter of a rectangle with sides (x + 3) and 2x. Simplify.
Stretch: Explain, with examples, why 3(x + 2) = 3x + 6 is an identity but 3(x + 2) = 15 is an equation.
exit: Simplify 6p + 2q − 4p + q
Classify x² + 1, x² + 1 = 10, x² ≥ 1
Return to the big question in one sentence.
lessons.homework: Eight questions on notation and vocabulary, including two worded 'form an expression' tasks.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: vocabulary card with example for each term; colour-code like terms. Stretch: the identity sign ≡ in context. Note: algebraic proof (A6) is taught in the school's 'Identities and algebraic proof' lesson.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: A1-A7 Algebra: notation, vocabulary and manipulation
lessons.title: Substituting into expressions and scientific formulae
lessons.bigQuestion: How do scientists use a formula to predict something that has not happened yet?
objectives: Substitute positive and negative numbers into expressions
Use formulae from science such as v = u + at and E = ½mv²
Follow the order of operations when substituting
successCriteria: All: substitute positive integers
Most: substitute negatives and powers correctly
Some: substitute into multi-variable formulae and interpret units
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: physics formulae for speed, force and energy
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: patterns and laws in nature expressed by formulae

keywords.def: replace letters with numbers
a rule using letters for quantities
work out the value
a letter that stands for a number that can change

teach.heading: Substituting carefully
bullets: Replace each letter with the number in brackets
teach.note: Write the substitution with brackets around negatives every time.

model.problem: Find the value of 2x² − x + 5 when x = −3

teach.heading: Scientific formulae
bullets: s = ut + ½at²: u = 3, a = 4, t = 2 → s = 14
State the unit in the answer
teach.note: Show the formula, substitution, answer layout. Square v before multiplying by ½m.

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: Square the number with its sign, not just the digit
teach.note: In calculators, enter (−3)² with brackets.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: Find 3x² when x = −2
check.why: x² = 4 first; then 3 × 4 = 12. A squares 3x; C treats the square as negative.

practice: Evaluate 3a + 2b when a = 4, b = −5
Evaluate x² − 2x + 1 when x = −4
F = ma. Find F when m = 12 and a = 3.5
s = ut + ½at². Find s when u = 3, a = 4, t = 2.
independent: Core: Evaluate (a) 5x − 2 for x = 3 (b) x² + 4 for x = −2 (c) 2x³ for x = 3
Extend: v² = u² + 2as. Find v when u = 6, a = 3 and s = 10, and when u = 6, a = −2 and s = 8.
Stretch: C = 5(F − 32)/9. Find C when F = 77 and find F when C = −40.
exit: Evaluate 3x − 4 when x = −2
Evaluate x² + 2x when x = −3
E = ½mv². Find E when m = 10 and v = 4.
lessons.homework: Ten substitutions including six scientific formulae from physics and chemistry class.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: substitution frame 'formula / replace / calculate / units'. Stretch: substitute algebraic expressions into formulae.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: A1-A7 Algebra: notation, vocabulary and manipulation
lessons.title: Expanding single brackets and factorising common factors
lessons.bigQuestion: Can you tell whether two different-looking expressions are the same?
objectives: Expand and simplify expressions with single brackets
Factorise expressions with a common factor
Factorise fully including letters
successCriteria: All: expand single brackets
Most: expand and simplify two brackets added or subtracted
Some: factorise fully expressions with powers and two letters
lessons.crossCurricular: Business: finding total costs; Computing: simplifying expressions
lessons.smsc: Social: working carefully so another person can follow your method

keywords.def: multiply out brackets
write as a product, putting common factors outside brackets
a factor shared by every term
the largest common factor

teach.heading: Expanding
bullets: Multiply every term inside by the term outside
teach.note: Use area models. Negative outside changes both signs inside.

model.problem: Expand and simplify 4(x + 3) − 2(x − 5)

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: A negative outside the bracket multiplies every term
teach.note: Check by substituting x = 2: left 4×5 − 2×(−3)=26. Right 2×2+22=26 ✓. The wrong version gives 4x + 12 − 2x − 10 = 2x + 2 which is 6.

teach.heading: Factorising
bullets: Find the highest common factor of all terms
Put it outside, work out what is left
teach.note: Expand your answer to check. Fully factorised means no common factor remains inside.

model.problem: Factorise fully 8a²b + 12ab²
steps: a is common, b is common: 4ab

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: Factorise fully 10x² + 15x
check.why: HCF is 5x. A leaves an x common; C is not integer coefficients; D multiplies wrongly.

practice: Expand 5(2x − 3) and −3(4 − x)
Expand and simplify 3(2x + 1) + 2(x − 4)
Factorise 14x + 21 and 9y² − 6y
Factorise fully 12a²b − 18ab²
independent: Core: (a) expand 4(x + 7) (b) factorise 10x − 25 (c) expand and simplify 2(x + 3) + 5(x − 1)
Extend: Expand and simplify x(x + 4) − 3(x − 2). Factorise 15x³ − 20x².
Stretch: Show that 3(2x − 1) − 2(3x − 4) is a constant for any value of x.
exit: Expand −4(2x − 3)
Factorise 6x² + 9x
Expand and simplify 5(x + 2) − 3(x − 1)
lessons.homework: Ten questions to expand, simplify and factorise, including a 'spot the error' on bracket signs.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: grid or area model for expansion; factor tree for HCF. Stretch: expanding double brackets is covered in the school's Year 10 'Expanding two and three binomials' lesson.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: Unit 10: Expressions, formulae and rearranging formulae
lessons.title: Rearranging formulae
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we make a different letter the subject of a formula?
objectives: To understand how to change the subject of a formula, including when the subject appears twice
successCriteria: All: change the subject of a formula with two steps
Most: rearrange formulae with powers and roots
Some: rearrange when the subject appears twice by factorising
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: v = u + at is rearranged to find the acceleration or the time
lessons.smsc: Algebra takes its name from al-jabr (الجبر) in the book of Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, written in Baghdad in the 9th century, and balancing both sides is the heart of rearranging

keywords.def: the letter on its own on one side of a formula
change which letter is the subject
the operation that undoes another
take out a common factor

hook.text: The formula F = 1.8C + 32 changes Celsius to Fahrenheit. How could you make a formula that goes the other way?
hook.a: Rearrange: subtract 32, then divide by 1.8: C = (F − 32)/1.8.

teach.heading: Like solving an equation
bullets: Do the same to both sides
teach.note: Pupils then make x the subject of y = 3x − 7.

model.problem: Make t the subject of v = u + at.

teach.heading: Powers and roots
bullets: Undo a square with a square root
teach.note: A = πr²: divide by π, then square root.

model.problem: Make r the subject of A = πr².

teach.heading: The subject twice
bullets: Collect subject terms on one side
teach.note: 4MA1 2.3A includes the subject appearing twice.

model.problem: Make x the subject of y = (x + 3)/(x − 2).

teach.heading: Common error
teach.note: Brackets show the whole of v − u is divided.

misconception.wrong: v = u + at gives t = v − u/a
misconception.right: t = (v − u)/a: the whole of v − u is divided by a

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: Make r the subject of C = 2πr.
check.why: Divide both sides by 2π. Subtracting 2π treats the multiplication as addition.

practice.q: Make x the subject of y = 3x − 7.
practice.model: Add 7 to both sides: y + 7 = 3x. Divide by 3: x = (y + 7)/3.

practice.q: Make w the subject of P = 2(l + w).
Make v the subject of E = ½mv² (v > 0).
Make t the subject of s = (u + v)t/2.

independent.q: Core: (a) Make v the subject of a = (v − u)/t (b) Make x the subject of y = 5 − 2x (c) Make h the subject of V = ⅓πr²h
independent.a: (a) v = u + at (b) x = (5 − y)/2 (c) h = 3V/(πr²)
independent.model: (a) Multiply by t: at = v − u; add u: v = u + at. (b) 2x = 5 − y, x = (5 − y)/2. (c) Multiply by 3: 3V = πr²h; divide by πr²: h = 3V/(πr²).

independent.q: Extend: Make x the subject of ax + 3 = bx − 5.
Stretch (exam style, 4 marks): Make x the subject of y = (2x + 1)/(x − 3).

exit.q: Make x the subject of y = (x − 4)/5.
Make b the subject of A = ½bh.
exit.a: b = 2A/h

exit.q: Big question: what extra step is needed when the subject appears twice?
exit.a: Collect the subject terms on one side and factorise to get the subject once.

lessons.homework: Rearrange C = (F − 32)/1.8 for F, s = ut + ½at² for a, and k = (m + 2)/(m − 1) for m.
lessons.send: Support: inverse operations flowchart. EAL: 'subject', 'rearrange'. Stretch: make l the subject of T = 2π√(l/g).
resources: Pearson International GCSE Mathematics A (4MA1) two-year scheme of work, Higher (the school's KS4 scheme): Unit 10 (4MA1 2.3A)

A circle with radius labelled

lessons.unit: A1-A7 Algebra: notation, vocabulary and manipulation
lessons.title: Functions and function notation
lessons.bigQuestion: How is a function like a machine with one input and one output?
objectives: Use function notation f(x) and f: x → …
Evaluate functions for given inputs
Solve f(x) = a to find inputs
successCriteria: All: evaluate f(x) for a number
Most: evaluate functions with squares and negatives
Some: solve equations of the form f(x) = k
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: functions with an input and a return value
lessons.smsc: Social: clear definitions make mathematical communication reliable

keywords.def: a rule that gives one output for each input
the number put into the function
the result of the function
the output of function f for input x

teach.heading: Function machines
bullets: f(x) = 3x + 2 means multiply by 3, then add 2
teach.note: Draw a flow diagram. Say 'f of 4' as 'the function f applied to 4'. Note this notation is used again when transforming graphs.

model.problem: f(x) = 2x² − 3. Find f(−3).

teach.heading: Solving f(x) = k
teach.note: Distinguish 'find f(5)' from 'find x when f(x) = 5'.

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: f(x) does not mean f times x
teach.note: Compare f(4) with 4f. For f(x) = 2x − 3, f(4) = 2(4) − 3 = 5.

misconception.right: f(3) means the output of the function when the input is 3

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: f(x) = 2x² − 3. What is f(−3)?
check.why: (−3)² = 9 so 2 × 9 − 3 = 15. B squares 2x first; C makes the square negative.

practice: f(x) = 5x − 4. Find f(3) and f(−2).
g(x) = x² + 1. Find g(4) and g(−3).
f(x) = 4x − 7. Solve f(x) = 13.
h(x) = x² − 5. Solve h(x) = 20.
independent: Core: f(x) = 3x + 1. Find f(2), f(0), f(−4) and solve f(x) = 19.
Extend: g(x) = (x + 3)/2. Find g(5) and g(−7). Solve g(x) = 6.
Stretch: f(x) = x² − 4x. Find all x with f(x) = 5. Find f(a + 1) in simplest form.
exit: f(x) = 4x − 1. Find f(5).
g(x) = x² − 2. Find g(−3).
Solve 3x + 2 = 20 using f(x) notation.
lessons.homework: Eight function evaluations, three of them solving f(x) = k, in the f: x → format as well.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: function machine diagrams; read the notation aloud. Stretch: the smallest value a quadratic function can take.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: A1-A7 Algebra: notation, vocabulary and manipulation
lessons.title: Composite and inverse functions
lessons.bigQuestion: Can every function be undone?
objectives: Find composite functions fg(x) and gf(x)
Find the inverse function f⁻¹(x)
Evaluate composite and inverse functions for a given input
successCriteria: All: evaluate a composite function for a value
Most: write a composite function algebraically
Some: find inverses including those with fractions
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: chaining functions in programs
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflection on order and reversal in everyday processes

keywords.def: a function applied after another, fg(x) = f(g(x))
undoes the original, f⁻¹
a value substituted into a function
the value the function gives

starter: Make x the subject of y = 3x − 4.

teach.heading: Composite functions
bullets: fg(x) means do g first, then f
teach.note: Emphasise the order: the function closest to x acts first. Show fg ≠ gf in general.

model.problem: f(x) = 2x + 1, g(x) = x². Find fg(3) and gf(x).

teach.heading: Inverse functions
bullets: Swap input and output, then rearrange
teach.note: Check: f(f⁻¹(x)) = x. The inverse of f(x) = (x + 5)/2 is f⁻¹(x) = 2x − 5.

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: fg means g is applied first
teach.note: Show with numbers.

misconception.right: fg(x) = f(g(x)); the function g acts first

teach.heading: Harder inverse
teach.note: Higher only. Collect x terms on one side then factorise.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: f(x) = x + 3 and g(x) = 2x. What is fg(x)?
check.why: g first: 2x, then add 3: 2x + 3. A is gf(x).

practice: f(x) = 3x, g(x) = x − 2. Find fg(x) and gf(x).
f(x) = x² and g(x) = x + 5. Find fg(2) and gf(2).
Find the inverse of f(x) = 4x + 7.
Find the inverse of g(x) = (x − 3)/5.
independent: Core: f(x) = x + 4, g(x) = 3x. (a) fg(2) (b) gf(2) (c) find f⁻¹(x)
Extend: f(x) = 2x − 5. Find f⁻¹(x) and ff(x). Solve f(x) = f⁻¹(x).
Stretch: f(x) = x + 2 and g(x) = x². Find x when fg(x) = gf(x).
exit: f(x) = x − 1, g(x) = 3x. Find fg(x).
Find the inverse of f(x) = 5x − 2.
Return to the big question: give a function with no inverse.
lessons.homework: Eight questions on composite functions, inverses, and ff(x), including one Higher-only fraction inverse.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: function machine chains with arrows backwards for inverses. Higher only: inverse of fractional functions.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: A8-A12 Algebra: graphs (linear, quadratic and standard curves)
lessons.title: Coordinates in four quadrants and plotting straight lines
lessons.bigQuestion: How can an equation be drawn as a picture?
objectives: Use coordinates in all four quadrants
Complete a table of values and plot a straight-line graph
Recognise lines such as x = a, y = b, y = x and y = −x
successCriteria: All: plot and read coordinates in four quadrants
Most: complete a table of values and draw a line
Some: decide whether a point lies on a line and find the midpoint of two points
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: map grid references; Computing: screen coordinates
lessons.smsc: Social: shared conventions let us locate places precisely

keywords.def: an ordered pair (x, y) giving a position
one of the four regions made by the axes
inputs and outputs used to plot a graph
the point (0, 0)

starter: Write down the coordinates of the origin.

teach.heading: Four quadrants
bullets: x first (across), then y (up or down)
The axes meet at the origin (0, 0)
teach.note: Ask pupils to place (−3, 2) and (2, −3) and see why order matters. Midpoint of (−2, 5) and (4, −1) is (1, 2): add and halve each coordinate.

teach.heading: Table of values
bullets: Plot the points and join with a ruler
Three points are enough; a fourth is a check
teach.note: Check that points lie in a straight line before drawing it.

model.problem: Draw y = 3x − 2 for x from −1 to 2
model.answer: A straight line through (0, −2) rising steeply

teach.heading: Special lines
bullets: x = 3 is vertical, every point has x = 3
teach.note: Use a graph tool to show each. The equation tells you what is true of every point on the line.

teach.heading: Common error
teach.note: Compare (4, 1) and (1, 4).

misconception.wrong: The point (−3, 2) is 2 across and 3 down
misconception.right: (−3, 2) means 3 to the left, then 2 up

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: Which point lies on y = 2x − 3?
check.why: 2 × 4 − 3 = 5. B gives 3, C gives −3, D gives −1.

practice: Write the coordinates of A, B, C if A is 2 right and 3 up from the origin, B is 4 left and 1 down, C is 3 right and 2 down.
Complete a table and plot y = 2x + 1 for x from −2 to 3
Find the midpoint of (−2, 5) and (4, −1)
Does (5, 12) lie on y = 2x + 1?
independent: Core: Plot y = x + 2 and y = −x on the same axes. Where do they cross?
Extend: Plot y = 2x − 3 and x + y = 6. Read the intersection.
Stretch: A(−3, 1), B(5, 1), C(5, 7) are three corners of a rectangle. Find D, the centre and the area.
exit: Complete a table for y = x − 3 with x = −2, 0, 3
Is (−1, −5) on y = 2x − 3? Show why.
Describe the line x = −4.
lessons.homework: Plot three lines on one set of axes and write down any shared points; two coordinate-geometry questions.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-drawn grids and a table template; the phrase 'along the corridor, up the stairs' for (x, y). Stretch: midpoint formula and length of a line segment.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: A8-A12 Algebra: graphs (linear, quadratic and standard curves)
lessons.title: Gradient and y = mx + c
lessons.bigQuestion: What does the number in front of x tell you about a line?
objectives: Calculate the gradient from two points
Read gradient and y-intercept from y = mx + c
Rearrange equations into y = mx + c
successCriteria: All: find the gradient from a graph
Most: identify m and c from an equation
Some: rearrange to y = mx + c and write an equation from a description
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: steepness of slopes; Engineering: roof pitch
lessons.smsc: Social: accuracy in a drawing so that others read it correctly

keywords.def: steepness: change in y ÷ change in x
where the line crosses the y-axis
change the form of an equation
gives a straight-line graph

starter: Bismillah. Plot (1, 2) and (3, 6) mentally and describe the move between them.

teach.heading: Gradient = rise ÷ run
bullets: Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x
Uphill is positive, downhill is negative
teach.note: Draw the triangle. Subtract coordinates in the same order top and bottom.

model.problem: Find the gradient of the line through (1, 2) and (5, 10)

teach.heading: y = mx + c
teach.note: Link to the table: c is y when x = 0.

teach.heading: Rearranging first
bullets: Gradient is the coefficient of x once y is alone
teach.note: Common slip: dividing only one term by the number.

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: The gradient is not the number on its own
teach.note: Pick y = 5x + 1: c is 1.

misconception.right: Rearrange: y = −2x + 5, so the gradient is −2

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: What is the gradient of 3y − 6x = 9?
check.why: 3y = 6x + 9, so y = 2x + 3. A has the wrong sign; C and D read a number from the equation.

practice: Find the gradient between (2, 3) and (6, 11)
State the gradient and intercept of y = −x + 4
Rearrange 3y = 12x − 6 and give m and c
Write the equation of the line with gradient −2 through (0, 3)
independent: Core: (a) gradient between (0, 1) and (4, 9) (b) gradient and intercept of y = ½x − 2 (c) write the equation with m = 4, c = −1
Extend: Rearrange 4x + 2y = 10 and 5y − 10x = 15; compare the lines.
Stretch: A line passes through (2, 5) and has gradient 3. Find its equation and where it meets the x-axis.
exit: Gradient between (1, 4) and (3, 10)
Gradient and intercept of y = 5 − 2x
Rearrange 2y = 6x + 8.
lessons.homework: Eight questions on gradients and y = mx + c, two with rearranging and one matching lines to graphs.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: the 'rise over run' staircase picture and sentence frame 'up ___ across ___'. Stretch: gradients as ratios of lengths.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: A8-A12 Algebra: graphs (linear, quadratic and standard curves)
lessons.title: Parallel lines and finding the equation of a line
lessons.bigQuestion: How many pieces of information do you need to fix one straight line?
objectives: Know that parallel lines have equal gradients
Find the equation of a line through a point with a given gradient
Find the equation of a line through two points
successCriteria: All: identify parallel lines from their equations
Most: find an equation through a point with a given gradient
Some: find an equation through two points with a fractional or negative gradient
lessons.crossCurricular: Engineering: parallel supports and slopes
lessons.smsc: Moral: reasoning from evidence, not guesswork

keywords.def: never meeting; same gradient
change in y ÷ change in x
put numbers in place of letters
the rule y = mx + c linking x and y on it

starter: Rearrange 2y = 4x + 5 to make y the subject.

teach.heading: Parallel lines
bullets: Parallel lines have the same gradient
teach.note: Ask pupils how they would show two lines are parallel without drawing them.

teach.heading: Through a point with a given gradient
bullets: Write y = mx + c, put in m
Substitute the point to find c
teach.note: Check that the point works in the final equation.

model.problem: Find the equation of the line through (−2, 5) and (2, −3)

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: Do not use the gradient of the original line unrearranged
teach.note: Rearrange y first.

misconception.right: y = 2x + 2.5, so the gradient is 2

teach.heading: Check

check.why: 3 ≥ 4 is false, so (2, 3) is on the wrong side. Shade the opposite side.

practice: Shade the region y ≤ x + 2
Shade the region where x ≥ 1, y ≥ 2 and x + y ≤ 7
State whether (3, 3) lies in the region y > x
How many integer points lie in the region x ≥ 1, y ≥ 2 and x + y ≤ 7 (boundary included)?
independent: Core: Draw and shade y < 3, x ≥ −1
Extend: Region R is y ≥ x, y ≤ 6 − x, x ≥ 0. Draw it and list the integer points inside it.
Stretch: A caterer makes x small boxes and y large boxes with x + y ≤ 40, x ≥ 5 and y ≥ 2x. Show the region and find the greatest number of large boxes.
exit: Is (1, 5) in the region y > 2x + 1?
Draw x + y < 4
Write two inequalities for the region below y = 3 and right of x = 1.
lessons.homework: Three graph-region questions on squared paper, one with a written explanation of how a test point is used.
lessons.send: Higher only. SEND/EAL: pre-drawn axes; colour shading or hatching; the phrase 'unwanted region shaded' for exam style. Stretch: linear programming.

lessons.unit: A23-A25 Algebra: sequences
lessons.title: Term-to-term and position-to-term rules
lessons.bigQuestion: If you know a pattern's rule, can you find the 100th term without listing 99 terms?
objectives: Generate terms from a term-to-term rule
Generate terms from a position-to-term rule (nth term)
Decide whether a number is a term of a sequence
successCriteria: All: continue a sequence using a rule
Most: use an nth term formula including n²
Some: test whether a number belongs to a sequence
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: loops and iteration; Art: pattern-making
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: pattern and order observed in nature and design

keywords.def: an ordered list of numbers following a rule
one number in a sequence
how to get the next term from the previous
uses the position n to find the term

teach.heading: Term-to-term rule
bullets: Rule: multiply by 2 then subtract 1, start 3
teach.note: Compute each step visibly. Slow, careful work.

model.problem: The nth term of a sequence is 3n + 2. Is 77 a term?

teach.heading: Position-to-term rule
teach.note: Highlight the difference between n (position) and the term itself.

teach.heading: Is it in the sequence?
bullets: n must be a positive integer
teach.note: This is a standard exam check; say the conclusion in a sentence.

teach.heading: Common error
teach.note: For n = 5: n² = 25.

misconception.right: The 5th term of n² is 5 × 5 = 25

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: The nth term is n² − 2n. What is the 3rd term?
check.why: 3² − 2(3) = 9 − 6 = 3. B squares only.

practice: First four terms of 4n − 1
First four terms when u₁ = 2 and the rule is 'double and subtract 3'
Is 50 a term of 4n − 2?
Find the 20th term of n² + 3
independent: Core: (a) terms 1 to 4 of 5n + 1 (b) term-to-term: start 4, add 7 (c) the 10th term of 2n − 3
Extend: Is 100 in 3n + 2? Is 100 in n² + 1? Which is the first term of n² − 5 to exceed 200?
Stretch: A sequence has u₁ = 3 and uₙ₊₁ = 2uₙ − 5. Find the first five terms.
exit: First three terms of 6n − 4
Is 41 a term of 5n + 1?
Start 2, rule 'multiply by 3': first four terms.
lessons.homework: Eight questions on generating terms and testing membership, including one with n².
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: tabular layout n / working / term; vocabulary glossary. Stretch: sequences defined by recurrence relations.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: A23-A25 Algebra: sequences
lessons.title: Special sequences: triangular, square, cube, Fibonacci-type and geometric
lessons.bigQuestion: What is the difference between adding the same amount each time and multiplying by the same amount each time?
objectives: Recognise triangular, square, cube, arithmetic, geometric and Fibonacci-type sequences
Continue geometric sequences and find a common ratio, including surd ratios (Higher)
Find missing terms in Fibonacci-type sequences
successCriteria: All: continue arithmetic and special sequences
Most: find the common ratio and continue a geometric sequence
Some: find unknowns in Fibonacci-type and geometric sequences including surds
lessons.crossCurricular: Biology: growth patterns; Art: spirals
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: patterns in creation and in human-made designs

keywords.def: a constant difference between terms
a constant ratio between terms
each term is the sum of the two before it
the multiplier between successive terms

starter: Bismillah. Write the first five square numbers.
Write the first four cube numbers.
What is the common difference in 7, 11, 15, ...?

teach.heading: Spot the type
teach.note: Triangular nth term n(n + 1)/2, so the 10th is 55. Squares n², cubes n³.

teach.heading: Geometric sequences
bullets: Common ratio r: divide a term by the one before
If the 2nd term is 6 and the 4th is 54, r² = 9
teach.note: Link r² when two steps apart: r = 3 gives first term 2 or r = −3 gives first term −2.

model.problem: A geometric sequence has second term 6 and fourth term 54, with positive terms. Find the first term.

teach.heading: Fibonacci-type
bullets: Each term = the sum of the previous two
If the 5th term is 21: 6 + 3x = 21, so x = 5
teach.note: Show the algebraic route to a missing term.

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: Ratio is found by dividing, not subtracting
teach.note: Differences do not work for geometric sequences.

misconception.wrong: 2, 6, 18 has common difference 4, so next is 22
misconception.right: 2, 6, 18 has common ratio 3, so next is 54

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: What is the next term of 5, 10, 20, 40?
check.why: The common ratio is 2 so the next term is 80. A and B continue by adding 10 and 20.

practice: Find r and the next two terms: 81, 27, 9, 3
Find missing terms of 1, ?, 4, 7, 11
A Fibonacci-type sequence starts 3, x, ... and the 5th term is 21. Find x.
independent: Core: (a) continue 4, 12, 36 (b) list the first six triangular numbers (c) write the first five cube numbers
Extend: Find the 10th triangular number and the sum of the first 4 cube numbers. Find r for 2, 2√2, 4 and the next term.
Stretch: A geometric sequence has second term 6 and fourth term 54. Find both possible first terms.
exit: Classify 2, 4, 8, 16
Continue 3, 3√3, 9, ...
Fibonacci-type: 2, 5, 7, 12: next term?
lessons.homework: Six classification and continuation questions, one with a surd ratio.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: table to record differences and ratios; Higher only for surd ratios. Stretch: sum of the first n triangular numbers.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier

lessons.unit: Unit 12: Sequences
lessons.title: Arithmetic sequences: nth term and sum
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we add up many terms of a sequence without listing them?
objectives: To understand how to use a + (n − 1)d for the nth term and find the sum of an arithmetic series
successCriteria: All: find the nth term of an arithmetic sequence
Most: find a and d from two terms and decide if a number is a term
Some: use Sn = n/2[2a + (n − 1)d] to solve problems
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: a loop that adds the same amount each time builds an arithmetic sequence
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: steady daily deeds add up

keywords.def: a sequence with a common difference
the first number in the sequence
the amount added each time
the sum of the terms of a sequence

hook.text: A pupil memorises 3 ayat on day 1, 5 on day 2, 7 on day 3 and so on. How could you find the total after 20 days without adding 20 numbers?
hook.a: Pair the first and last: (3 + 41) × 20 ÷ 2 = 440. The formula Sn does this.

teach.heading: The formula
bullets: a: first term; d: common difference

teach.heading: Finding a and d
bullets: The gap in positions × d = the gap in values

model.problem: The 5th term is 23 and the 12th term is 51. Find a and d.

teach.heading: Sum of a series
teach.note: Pairing first and last terms always gives the same total.

model.problem: Find the sum of the first 20 terms of 7, 11, 15, ...

teach.heading: Common error
teach.note: The 1st term has had no differences added.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: What is the nth term of 20, 17, 14, ...?
check.why: 20 − 3(n − 1) = 23 − 3n. 20 − 3n gives 17 as the first term.

practice.q: Find the nth term of 5, 12, 19, ...
practice.model: a = 5, d = 7. nth term = 5 + 7(n − 1) = 7n − 2. Check: n = 2 gives 12.

practice.q: Find the 50th term of 3n + 8.
Find the sum of the first 10 terms of 2, 5, 8, ...
Is 100 a term of 6n − 4?

independent.q: Core: For 13, 9, 5, 1, ... find (a) the nth term (b) the 30th term (c) the sum of the first 15 terms
Extend (exam style, 4 marks): The 4th term of an arithmetic sequence is 17 and the 9th term is 42. Find the sum of the first 20 terms.
Stretch: How many terms of 3, 7, 11, ... are needed for the sum to exceed 1000?
independent.a: Sn = n(2n + 1). n = 22 gives 990; n = 23 gives 1081. So 23 terms

exit.q: Find the nth term of 9, 15, 21, ...
Find the sum of the first 5 terms of 9, 15, 21, ...
Big question: how does pairing terms help find a sum?
exit.a: First + last, second + second last, and so on, all give the same total, so Sn = n/2 × (first + last).

lessons.homework: Answer the hook: find the total ayat after 20 days, and the day on which the running total first passes 600.
lessons.send: Support: a, d, n labelled on each sequence. EAL: 'series', 'common difference'. Stretch: prove Sn = n/2[2a + (n − 1)d] by writing the sum forwards and backwards.
resources: Pearson International GCSE Mathematics A (4MA1) two-year scheme of work, Higher (the school's KS4 scheme): Unit 12 (4MA1 3.1A to 3.1C)

pictures.alt: Cans stacked in rows that decrease by one
An open mushaf on a stand, for the daily hifdh plan

lessons.unit: A23-A25 Algebra: sequences
lessons.title: The nth term of a quadratic sequence
lessons.bigQuestion: What happens when the differences are not constant but their differences are?
objectives: Recognise a quadratic sequence from second differences
Find the nth term an² + bn + c
Check the formula and use it
successCriteria: All: find first and second differences
Most: find a quadratic nth term when a is a whole number
Some: handle a = 1.5 and remainders that are linear
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: distance under constant acceleration
lessons.smsc: Social: checking a general result against known cases

keywords.def: the difference of the first differences
has a constant second difference
formula for the term in position n
what is left after subtracting an²

starter: Bismillah. Find the differences between consecutive terms of 2, 5, 10, 17.
List the first five square numbers.

teach.heading: Second differences
teach.note: Half of the second difference is the coefficient a: 4 ÷ 2 = 2, so 2n².

model.problem: Find the nth term of 3, 9, 19, 33, 51

teach.heading: Linear remainder
teach.note: Check with n = 4: 32 + 4 − 1 = 35 ✓.

teach.heading: Halves
teach.note: Show the second difference 3 gives a = 1.5.

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: a is half the second difference
teach.note: For second difference 4, a = 2 not 4.

misconception.right: Second difference 6 means 3n²

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: A sequence has a constant second difference of 6. What is a in an² + bn + c?

practice: Find the nth term of 4, 7, 12, 19, 28
Find the nth term of 3, 9, 19, 33
Find the nth term of 2, 9, 20, 35
State the 10th term of n² + 3
independent: Core: (a) second differences of 2, 5, 10, 17 (b) nth term
Extend: nth term of 5, 14, 29, 50 and of 0, 6, 16, 30
Stretch: A sequence has nth term 1.5n² + n. Find the first three terms and the first differences, and explain why the second difference is 3.
exit: nth term of 2, 8, 18, 32
nth term of 5, 8, 13, 20
Second difference of 4n² + 1
lessons.homework: Six quadratic nth term problems, two with a ≠ 1 and one worded about a pattern of dots.
lessons.send: Higher only. SEND/EAL: difference table template; Stretch: cubic sequences.

lessons.unit: R1-R8: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: units, scale and ratio
lessons.title: Converting standard and compound units
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does 1 m² not equal 100 cm²?
objectives: Convert between metric units of length, mass, capacity and time
Convert area and volume units
Convert compound units such as km/h to m/s, numerically and algebraically
successCriteria: All: convert lengths, masses and capacities
Most: convert areas, volumes and speeds
Some: convert compound units in algebraic expressions
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: converting g/cm³ to kg/m³ and m/s to km/h
lessons.smsc: Adab of precision: honest measurement and fair weights are stressed in the Qur'an (55:9: 'And establish weight in justice and do not make deficient the balance').

keywords.def: the number you multiply or divide by to change units
a unit made from two others, such as km/h
a unit in the metric system such as m, kg, l

starter: Bismillah. Work out 3.5 km in metres.
Write 0.45 as a fraction in its simplest form.

teach.heading: The metric facts to recall
bullets: Length: 10 mm in 1 cm, 100 cm in 1 m
Mass: 1000 g in 1 kg, 1000 kg in 1 tonne
Capacity: 1000 ml in 1 litre, 1 cm³ is 1 ml
Time: 60 s in 1 min, 60 min in 1 hour
